title: Called up to the Torah
hookLine: people are called up to say a blessing before and after each section

cards: It's Shabbat morning. The scroll is open on the reading table, and the room goes quiet. Someone at the table calls out a Hebrew name, the person's own and their parents'.
A person in the congregation stands up, a little nervous, and walks to the front. Maybe it's their first time since their bar or bat mitzvah. Maybe their grandmother is watching.
Maybe they've just had a baby, or are about to get married, or it's the anniversary of a parent's death. They step up to the scroll. They don't have to read a word of it.

teach.b: The word is aliyah, going up. The reading table often stands on a raised platform, the bimah, so you literally go up to it. But the word means more than stairs: being called to the Torah is an honor, a going up in spirit.

teach.h: SEVEN ON SHABBAT, THREE ON WEEKDAYS.
teach.b: On Shabbat morning the portion is divided into seven sections, and seven people are called, one for each, with an extra one at the end. On Mondays and Thursdays, three.
Traditionally the first goes to a kohen, a descendant of the priests, the second to a levi, and the rest to anyone. Here's what happens.
The person looks at the place in the scroll and says the blessing before. It begins Barchu, bless the Lord who is blessed, and it thanks God for choosing Israel and giving the Torah.
The reader chants the section while the person stands beside them, following along.

teach.h: A TORAH OF TRUTH, ETERNAL LIFE.
teach.b: Then the blessing after: thanking God, who gave us a Torah of truth and planted eternal life in our midst. And they step aside for the next. In Orthodox synagogues, men are called up.

In Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative synagogues, women are called up too. The same word has another life: when a Jew moves to the land of Israel, that's also called making aliyah, going up.
So this week's four days fit together: a handwritten scroll, heard aloud. Fifty-four portions. A way to read one.
And now, a way to stand beside it, and go up.

how: During the Torah reading, members of the congregation are called by their Hebrew names to recite blessings before and after each section while the reader chants; seven are called on Shabbat morning and three on Mondays and Thursdays.

games.q: your Hebrew name has just been called. you walk up to the open scroll. what do you do first?
o: look at the place and say the blessing before.
roll the scroll to your favorite passage.
games.why: you look at the place and bless. the reader chants; you stand beside, then bless again after.

practice: Picture a book or a page you'll read today, and imagine standing up and walking toward it, as if your name had been called. If you pray, you can say the old words, blessed are you, Lord our God, who gave us a Torah of truth.
If you don't, just stand, or sit up straight, and take one breath of respect before the first word.

wordCard.voice: Aliyah. Going up: being called to the Torah to say the blessings before and after a section of the reading.
